I. MPA PROGRAM STRATEGIC CONTEXT
1. The Accelerating Access to Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene in the Eastern and Southern Africa Region
using the Multiphase Programmatic Approach (AFE WASH MPA) was approved on 30 September 2025 with a financing envelope of US$ 1,580 million (Report No: PADHI01078). The AFE WASH MPA comprises one regional operation and 12 country operations in Angola, Burundi, Comoros, Democratic Republic of Congo
(DRC), Ethiopia, Malawi, Madagascar, Mozambique, Somalia, South Sudan, Tanzania, and Zambia. The first regional WASH project (P506439) and Tanzania operation (P508698) were approved on September 30, 2025;
Burundi (P507207) on December 10, 2025; and Comoros (P514166) on March 24, 2025.
2. Eastern and Southern Africa faces a deepening WASH crisis that constrains economic growth, human capital,
and jobs. In 2022, 277 million people lacked basic water services and 458 million lacked basic sanitation, disproportionately affecting rural poor households, women and girls, and populations in FCV settings.
Inadequate WASH services cost an estimated 5 percent of regional GDP annually, contribute to stunting, and reinforce gender inequalities. Addressing these gaps requires stronger governance, climate-resilient service delivery, and increased private financing. Through country-led investments and sector reforms, the AFE WASH
MPA directly advances the WBG’s Water Forward, Jobs, Gender, and FCV priorities.
3. Water Forward seeks to advance water security for 1 billion people by 2030, including 400 million reached
by the WBG through the Water Strategy Implementation Plan (WSIP), approved in December 2025. The AFE
WASH MPA supports the Water Strategy Implementation Plan’s Water for People pillar, which targets basic
WASH access for 250 million people by 2030, through country-led investments and reforms anchored in national Compacts. The DRC: Scaling Up Water Supply and Sanitation Access in Kinshasa Project (P513301) is a flagship operation of the WASH MPA, accounting for around 25% of the MPA water supply access target.
Through investments in utility performance improvement, sector governance reforms, mobilization of private capital through PPPs, and expanded water and sanitation access in Kinshasa, the project directly advances all four pillars of the regional MPA and strengthens achievement of the MPA’s access and systems-change objectives.
II. MPA PROGRAM DESCRIPTION
A. Program Development Objective and Indicators
4. The Program Development Objective (PrDO) is to increase access to climate-resilient water supply, sanitation,
and hygiene services in participating Eastern and Southern African countries. The MPA applies a common framework to expand household and institutional WASH access. No PrDO results are yet reported, as the FY26 operations became effective only on February 19, 2026 (Tanzania), March 30, 2026 (Burundi), and June 9, 2026
(Comoros).

B. Program Theory of Change
5. The theory of change for the program remains unchanged.
C. Program Beneficiaries
6. Program beneficiaries remain unchanged: across the 12 participating countries, the MPA will provide at least
basic water services to 17 million people, basic sanitation to 13 million people, and WASH services to 7,500 schools and health care facilities; already approved operations account for 3.8 million water beneficiaries, 4.6 million sanitation beneficiaries, and 2,300 institutional WASH facilities. The DRC: Scaling Up Water Supply and
Sanitation Access in Kinshasa Project accounts for 4.2 million water beneficiaries and 100 institutional WASH facilities.
D. Program Description
7. The AFE WASH MPA structure consists of four pillars or Program Components encompassing the overall
scope of the Program and covering urban and rural, water and sanitation sub-sectors. The four pillars contain a comprehensive menu of activities that is tailored to the needs and priorities of participating countries. The participating countries select indicators across a menu of indicators to measure the results for the various program components
8. Pillar 1: WASH Acceleration Platforms. This component establishes regional and government-led national
platforms to coordinate stakeholders around multi-year WASH Investment Plans anchored in National WASH
Compacts. It promotes budget prioritization, cross-country learning, and stronger sector M&E and data systems, with AUDA-NEPAD providing capacity-building and partnership support.
9. Pillar 2: Sector Governance Reforms. This component strengthens governance, transparency, and
accountability by updating policies and laws, clarifying mandates, reinforcing decentralized service delivery and institutional capacity, and improving regulatory functions, tariff frameworks, and formalization of local
The World Bank
Accelerating Access to Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in the Eastern and Southern Africa Region (P512763) –
Phase 4
Page 3 providers. Regional tools, knowledge exchange, and analytical reviews will inform national investment planning.
10. Pillar 3: Improving Service Provision Performance. This component strengthens the sustainability, financial
viability, and climate resilience of urban and rural WASH services. It supports utility performance improvement, digitalization, energy efficiency, creditworthiness, inclusive sanitation, rural service professionalization, market-based sanitation, smart subsidies, behavior change, and skills development for women and youth, while strengthening information systems, customer engagement, renewable energy use, and private-sector innovation.
11. Pillar 4: Financing Climate-Resilient Water Supply and Sanitation (WSS) Infrastructure and Promoting Private
Sector Participation. This pillar finances climate-resilient WASH infrastructure in urban and rural areas, including schools, health centers, and rural sanitation, while mobilizing private and innovative finance through blended structures, Public Private Partnerships (PPPs), risk mitigation instruments, microfinance, and climate finance in partnership with IFC and MIGA. It addresses financing constraints for utilities and service providers, supports WASH budget allocations, and strengthens water security through flood and drought management, storage, aquifer recharge, water reuse, and transboundary groundwater planning.
E. Program Framework
12. Principles of country engagement. Achieving universal WASH access in AFE requires substantial investment
amid limited fiscal space. In response to country demand, the MPA supports 12 countries in establishing government-led WASH programs with time-bound access targets, credible financing plans, and reforms anchored in national WASH Compacts. These programs address governance constraints and mobilize private financing. The DRC WASH Compact aligns with the Program framework by advancing governance reforms, utility efficiency, and scaled-up financing, including private capital.
13. The AFE WASH MPA will be implemented over eight years, from September 2025 to September 2033. Four
of the 12 countries joined in FY26; the remaining eight are expected to join in FY27–FY28, allowing sufficient time to meet their targets. Since Board approval, operational and country-context changes have resulted in the following adjustments, with no changes yet in the Board approved MPA financing envelope (IBRD and IDA)
of US$1,580 million.
• Burundi (P507207): Other financing decreased from US$15 million to US$10 million; IDA financing
remains US$80 million.
• Comoros (P514166): Approval advanced from December 2026 to March 2026; risk lowered from
Substantial to Moderate; IDA financing increased from US$20 million to US$29 million; and other financing of US$10 million was not mobilized.
• DRC (P513301): Approval shifting from July to November 2026; IDA financing increased from US$200
million to US$250 million, and other financing increased from US$300 million to US$325 million.
• South Sudan (P518890): Approval delayed from March 2026 to February 2027.
• Ethiopia (P516998): Approval delayed from September 2026 to February 2027; IDA financing increased
from US$200 million to US$350 million; other financing increased from US$185 million to US$255.5 million.
• Angola (P518656): Approval advanced from March to February 2027; IBRD financing increased from
US$240 million to US$350.9 million; other financing increased from US$210 million to US$1,350 million
• Madagascar (P-number not yet assigned): Approval delayed from September 2026 to FY27/FY28.
The World Bank

• Somalia (P-number not yet assigned): Approval delayed from September 2026 to FY27/FY28.
• Regional operations: Second and third regional project implemented by AUDA-NEPAD delayed and
contingent on progress under the first regional operation(P506439).
F. Learning Agenda
14. No learning agenda findings are available, as MPA and regional operation implementation has only recently
begun. The learning agenda remains unchanged from the PAD.
G. Program Implementation
15. Country operations. Each country operation is implemented by designated national agencies, consistent with
the country’s institutional framework. A governance body provides strategic oversight, coordinates sector institutions, and approves annual work plans and budgets, while a Project Management Unit manages day-to-
day implementation, fiduciary and environmental and social functions, results monitoring, and capacity building.
16. Regional project. AUDA-NEPAD implements the regional project through its Project Implementation Unit,
which manages regional technical assistance, knowledge exchange, benchmarking, and support for country reforms. A Regional Project Advisory Committee provides strategic coordination and agrees on joint regional activities, while Country Coordination Teams in the 12 participating countries identify demand and coordinate delivery of regional support. Their respective roles are defined in the Project Operations Manual.
H. Overall Program Risk
17. The overall Program risk remains Substantial, with no change in the risks to achieving the PrDO.

@#&OPS~Doctype~OPS^dynamics@padlegalcovenants#doctemplate
LEGAL
Legal Covenants
Sections and Description
Schedule 2, section I.A.3(a): No later than three (3) months after the Effective Date, recruit or assign to the CEP-O, an environmental and social manager and an occupational health and safety specialist, with experience, qualifications, and skills and under terms of reference acceptable to the Association.
Schedule 2, section I.A.2: No later than three (3) months after the Effective Date, or such later date as agreed by the
Association, establish and maintain at all times during Project implementation, a high-level inter-ministerial steering committee (the “Project Steering Committee”), with a structure, functions, and responsibilities acceptable to the
Association, which shall be responsible for overall Project oversight and strategic guidance and approving Annual Work
Plans and Budgets. The Project Steering Committee shall be chaired by the MRHE represented by the Secretary General of the MRHE. The Project Steering Committee shall be co-chaired by the Secretary General of the MEDDNEC and shall include representatives from the Presidency, the Prime Minister’s Office, from the Recipient’s ministries in charge of finance, planning, portfolio, health, education, urbanism and housing, land, City of Kinshasa, REGIDESO, ARSPE and CEP-
O coordinator.

I. STRATEGIC CONTEXT
A. Country Context
1. The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) possesses significant economic potential, underpinned by its
vast natural resources, abundant water resources, and a population of approximately 109 million.1 These demographic and resource endowments present opportunities for job creation and private investment. DRC has
52 percent of all freshwater resources and 23 percent of internal renewable water resources in Sub-Saharan
Africa.2 Despite its potential, the DRC remains one of the world's poorest countries, with an extreme poverty rate of 72.9 percent and a Human Development Index ranking of 179 out of 191.3 More than half of the DRC’s impoverished population resides in and around major urban areas.4 The country faces widespread gender inequality and high rates of violence against women.
2. Unlocking DRC’s potential requires addressing persistent infrastructure gaps, institutional fragility,
governance challenges, and regulatory constraints. Economic growth during 2020-24, averaged over 6.4 percent, yet gains in per capita income and poverty reduction have remained limited due to rapid population growth and dependence on the mining sector. Although poverty has declined from 78.9 percent of Congolese in
2020 to an estimated 72.9 percent in 2024,5 the figure remains exceedingly high. Converting resource-driven growth into broad-based improvements in living standards and access to basic services remains a major challenge.
3. DRC has an urbanization rate of approximately 44.5 percent but is urbanizing at income levels
significantly below global comparators. The capital Kinshasa is a densely populated and fast-growing city of over
17 million people (2021),6 concentrating the highest number of people living in poverty compared to any other province in the DRC. About 12 million Kinshasa inhabitants live in poverty. Moreover, Kinshasa's population is growing faster than that of other urban areas, at 5.1 per cent per year, compared to a national population growth of nearly 3.2 per cent. It could exceed 20 million inhabitants in 2030.7
4. DRC is highly vulnerable to climate change, with major implications for people, infrastructure, and
ecosystems. DRC ranks as the 21st most vulnerable country and the fifth least ready to adapt, according to the
Notre Dame Global Adaptation Initiative Country Index.8 The country faces multiple climate change-exacerbated hazards, of which rainfall-triggered floods and landslides are the most prevalent. The DRC’s Country Climate and
Development Report (CCDR)9 concludes that climate change is already increasing temperatures and rainfall variability – trends expected to intensify over time. More frequent extreme events disproportionately affect poor and vulnerable households, communities, small businesses, and governments, exacerbating poverty through damage to livelihoods, infrastructure, and productive assets. These hazards disrupt water services, damage infrastructure, and increase the incidence of waterborne diseases such as cholera, underscoring the need for climate-resilient infrastructure and services.

B. Sectoral and Institutional Context
5. Due to the vast resources of the Congo basin and a high average annual rainfall of over 1,500 mm per
year, the DRC is water rich. Internal renewable freshwater resources per capita are estimated at 12,213 m3/person (2017),10 significantly above the internationally recognized water sufficiency threshold of 1,700 m3/person/year. Despite this abundance, access to safe and reliable water remains a challenge for many
Congolese citizens. The total volume of freshwater withdrawn by major economic sectors is only about 0.2 percent of the total resource endowment. Decades of conflict, underinvestment, and lack of connectivity across the DRC’s vast territory have resulted in significant infrastructure gaps which are major constraints to sustainable and inclusive growth.
6. The DRC has the largest population in Sub-Saharan Africa without access to water, and third-largest
population after Nigeria and Ethiopia, lacking access to sanitation, and hygiene (WASH). As of 2024, about 70 million people (64 percent) lack basic water access, 91 million people lack basic sanitation (84 percent), and 88 million people lack basic hygiene services (81 percent).11 Kinshasa in particular is facing a severe water supply and sanitation crisis, as population growth continuously surpasses the pace of service expansion. More than 8 million people in the city (48 percent) do not have access to basic water supply. The proportion of households with access to piped water, mostly outdoors, declined from about 72 percent in 2018 to 52 percent in 2022.12
7. Kinshasa’s water supply system is under severe strain with only about 60 percent of current demand
met. The city relies primarily on two major water treatment plants (WTP) located in the central part of the city:
the aging N’djili WTP (330,000 m³/day capacity) and the recently commissioned Ozone WTP (330,000 m³/day).
The Ozone plant draws water from the Congo river, but N’djili WTP suffers frequent breakdowns due to obsolete equipment, flooding, and severe pollution of the N’djili river. Additional smaller plants, such as Lemba-Imbu,
Ngaliema, Lukunga and Lukaya, operate at limited capacity and face recurrent outages due to similar challenges.
Overall, the city faces a severe water production deficit of more than 500,000m3/day to meet current demand, and the deficit is projected to exceed 1,200,000 m3/day by 2035.13 The city’s water supply infrastructure is characterized by aging assets, uneven coverage, and vulnerability to climate shocks, leaving peri-urban areas underserved. The eastern, western and southern parts of the city have very limited water supply infrastructure.
8. The Government of DRC prepared a 2020-2030 National Program for Water, Sanitation and Hygiene
(Programme National d’Eau, Hygiène et Assainissement, PNEHA). It lays out investments required – estimated at US$8 billion – to reach the ambitious access targets of 80 percent for urban water, 60 percent for rural water,
70 percent for sanitation and universal access in schools and health centers by 2030. A mid-term review of the
PNEHA held in October 2025, facilitated by the National Action Committee for Water Supply, Sanitation, and
Hygiene (CNAEHA, Committée Nationale d’Action, d’Eau, Hygiène et Assaisinissement), showed that progress is lagging behind due to inadequate investment. To reinforce reform momentum and mobilize investment, the
Government launched the DRC WASH Compact (Pacte Présidentiel Eau–Hygiène–Assainissement) in 2026. The

Compact sets intermediate targets for 2035 of 60 percent access to drinking water, 50 percent access to sanitation and hygiene services, and 80 percent WASH coverage in schools and health facilities (equivalent to reaching an additional 69 million people with at least basic services), as milestones toward universal access by
2050. It combines governance, utility performance, financial sustainability, and private sector reforms with a
sector financing strategy requiring an estimated US$20 billion in investments over 2026–2035. The Compact identifies a financing gap of approximately US$14.7 billion, highlighting the need for increased public, donor, private, and climate-related financing.
9. Public spending for WASH is low and budget execution rates are insufficient, leaving the sector
dependent on donor financing. An analysis of expenditure data over the 2017-2021 period reveals that domestic public expenditure on WASH was only 0.23 percent of overall government expenditure (excluding external funds), a mere 0.02 percent of GDP and in absolute terms only US$9 million on average annually, of which just
15 percent for investments. Donor-financed expenditure is tenfold, at US$93 million on average annually, mostly off budget. Domestic budget execution rates are low at around 20 percent.14
10. The regulatory and governance framework for the water and sanitation sector in the DRC has recently
undergone significant reforms, yet important challenges remain. The establishment of the Autorité de
Régulation du Secteur de l’Eau Potable et de l’Assainissement (ARSPE) as the sector regulator in 2022 marked an important step toward stronger oversight, transparency, and accountability.15 However, ARSPE remains at an early stage of operationalization. The recent appointment of its key officials and approval of its operating manual by the Board of Directors have established the foundations for the Agency to progressively assume its regulatory functions.16 Public-Private Partnerships (PPP) in the sector are governed by PPP Law No. 18/016 of July 9, 2018 and Water Law No. 15/026 of December 31, 2015, which permit private participation and define procedures for project preparation, procurement, and contract management. However, inconsistencies remain between the two laws, particularly regarding Public Service Delegation arrangements. A new PPP law is under preparation, which should address these inconsistencies.17 PPPs are managed by the Coordination and Advisory Unit on
Public-Private Partnerships (UC-PPP, Unité de Conseil et de Coordination des Partenariats Public-Privé) under the
Ministry of Planning.18 While UC-PPP is responsible for implementing PPP policy, promoting and monitoring projects, and advising contracting authorities, practical implementation is still nascent. Capacity building, standardized tools, and stronger coordination among UC-PPP, ARSPE, and sector ministries are needed. The regulatory environment for PPPs—particularly regarding risk allocation, fiscal commitments, and dispute resolution—requires further support to attract and sustain private sector participation.
11. The Government is reforming key state-owned enterprises responsible for service delivery, including the
national water utility (Régie de Distribution d’Eau – REGIDESO). Established in 1929, REGIDESO is a public company whose historic mission is to ensure access to drinking water for all citizens. REGIDESO was restructured into a public limited company (Société Anonyme) on September 4, 2014, with the Congolese State as its sole shareholder. It enjoys corporate legal status and is subjected to fiscal oversight by the Ministry of Portfolio, while its technical operations are overseen by the Ministry of Water Resources and Electricity (Ministère des Ressources
Hydrauliques et de l’Électricité, MRHE). The Board of Directors and the Managing Director are appointed by the

Page 20
State, with the latter most recently selected through a competitive recruitment process. This transformation is part of a broad effort to rebuild the institutional landscape of the water sector, consolidated in Water Law 2015.
12. Currently, REGIDESO develops and manages drinking water production and distribution in 101 urban
centers across the DRC’s 26 provinces but faces severe operational and financial challenges. National service coverage remains critically low at 16 percent, with non-revenue water (NRW) at approximately 38 percent in
2026. Kinshasa is the anchor of REGIDESO's operational and financial sustainability: the capital accounts for
roughly 60 percent of the utility's 411,000 active customer accounts, generates a 36 percent operating surplus that cross-subsidizes a 52 percent operating loss across other provinces, and outperforms the rest of the network on service coverage (approximately 50 percent) and NRW (35 percent). This cross-subsidization mechanism, supported by public investment subsidies, underpins the utility's ability to maintain a financially viable tariff structure while extending services nationwide. Thus, improvements in Kinshasa's service quality, revenue collection, and NRW reduction are essential to REGIDESO's overall viability. The utility’s financial sustainability is further undermined by chronic non-payment of government water bills, with arrears exceeding US$600 million, contributing to infrastructure degradation, elevated water losses, and limited capacity to expand or maintain services, particularly for vulnerable households.
13. In response, REGIDESO’s management is implementing a comprehensive performance improvement
plan (PIP), under a performance contract signed with the Government in December 2023, leveraging digitalization and operational innovations to strengthen efficiency and accountability. Early results are promising, with revenue collection rising from approximately CDF 270 billion in 2020 to CDF 470 billion in 2024, and NRW reducing from 43 percent in 2022. These gains have significantly enhanced stakeholder confidence in the utility and the sector, helping create the conditions for the Government to approve a major tariff increase in March
2026.19 The tariff adjustment is expected to improve cost recovery and restore REGIDESO’s financial sustainability while preserving targeted social protection measures for vulnerable consumers. It was implemented under the tariff-setting and adjustment framework adopted in July 2024, which established the principles and procedures for future tariff revisions.20 Sustaining REGIDESO’s transformation will require continued Government commitment to the performance contract, tariff reforms, and stronger sector governance, supported by targeted investments and technical assistance. In particular, a credible tariff indexation mechanism, together with measures to reduce Government arrears and strengthen payment discipline, will be critical to improving operational performance and ensuring long-term financial sustainability.
14. The urban sanitation sector in Kinshasa operates within a complex institutional framework involving
multiple city-level entities and faces significant challenges in service delivery, regulation, and financing. Key actors include the Régie d’Assainissement de Kinshasa (RASKIN), which oversees urban sanitation services; the
Régie de Gestion des Déchets de Kinshasa (REGEDEK), which is responsible for primary waste collection; the Fonds d’Assainissement de Kinshasa (FONAK), which is responsible for mobilizing and managing financing for sanitation activities; and the Brigade Spéciale pour la Protection de l’Environnement (BSPE), which monitors and supervises sanitation projects and activities. These entities operate under the authority of the City of Kinshasa. The Cellule de Développement Urbain de Kinshasa (CDUK) is responsible for urban planning and development across the city.
Collectively, these institutions operate under the policy guidance of the Ministère de l’Environnement, du
Développement durable et de la Nouvelle Économie du Climat (MEDDNEC) through the Direction de l’Assainissement (DAS). Strengthening their capacity and coordination is essential for improving sanitation outcomes in the city. A Citywide Inclusive Sanitation (CWIS) masterplan for Kinshasa is nearing completion, with support from the KIN ELENDA Project (P171141). This masterplan includes the identification of required institutional reforms and prescribes both sewered and non-sewered solutions to sanitation management,

It also incorporates priority investments, including a Fecal Sludge Treatment Plant (FSTP) to be financed under this project.
15. The project will consolidate and build on the recent gains and reforms in the sector by expanding access
to safe water and sanitation services in underserved areas of Kinshasa while strengthening the institutional foundations for sustainable service delivery. It builds on the achievements of the water component of the
Kinshasa Multisector Development and Urban Resilience Project (KIN ELENDA, P171141), which has financed additional water production capacity at the Ozone plant complex, network expansion, and utility reforms, benefiting more than 2 million people in Kinshasa. The project also complements the broader sector reform agenda supported by the DRC Water Supply and Sanitation Access Program (PASEA, P178389) and the Access,
Governance and Reform of the Electricity and Water Sectors Project (AGREE, P173506) project, by providing additional support to accelerate the REGIDESO’s transformation program, advance PPP preparation, and strengthen urban sanitation sector institutions. In addition, the project aligns with the Inga3 Development
Program (P506438), through the expansion of water infrastructure and services in the Inga Growth Corridor and specifically the Maluku Special Economic Zone.
C. Relevance to Higher Level Objectives
16. The project is aligned with the objectives of the World Bank’s Country Partnership Framework (CPF) for
DRC for FY22-26 (Report No. 168084-ZR), particularly Focus Area 2, Objective 2.2, by expanding access to WASH services for underserved populations and reducing the burden on women and girls. It is also well-positioned to contribute to the forthcoming CPF under preparation for FY2027–2036 (P516836, PCN approved), which adopts an integrated corridor approach — “Three Corridors for More and Better Jobs” (3C4J) centered on the Inga,
Lobito, and Peace Corridors as zones for economic transformation, improved connectivity, private investment, and job creation. The project's support for WASH access, institutional strengthening, and gender-responsive service delivery aligns with the new CPF's outcome of Connected Markets and Communities. The project is further aligned with the 2025 DRC Risk and Resilience Assessment (RRA)21 by addressing FCV drivers such as rapid urbanization and youth unemployment through investments that support economic transformation, private sector participation, and job creation. The robust reform package supported by Component 1 directly addresses elite capture of the state undermining service delivery and the accountability gap between the state and citizens
(RRA driver 1). The project's youth employment agenda reflected in the results framework contributes to addressing socioeconomic marginalization and youth vulnerability to recruitment into violence (RRA driver 2).
The project thus advances the CPF cross-cutting priorities of climate, gender, and governance.
17. The project is aligned with the Mobilizing Finance for Development (MFD) principles and applies a one
World Bank Group (WBG) approach, working closely with IFC and MIGA under the Scaling-Up Water Finance initiative.22 Private investment generated through the project will count toward Private Capital Mobilization
(PCM).23 Component 1 is verified as MFD-enabling through its support for sector reforms, the regulatory framework, and REGIDESO’s performance improvement program, including exploration of a NRW performance-
based contract. The project will also finance studies to mobilize private financing for local manufacturing of sector equipment, such as pipes, pumps, and valves, supporting import substitution and long-term sustainability.
Under subcomponent 2.2, sludge collection for the FSTP is also verified as MFD-enabling, as private operators are expected to lease trucks and collect fees directly from households. For PCM, the project includes a hybrid
PPP for bulk-water production facilities in Lukunga, with REGIDESO serving as off-taker. A PPP feasibility study

Page 22 estimates the cost of this subproject at about US$87 million, with a preliminary assessment indicating a US$37 million viability gap fund (VGF) to be fully financed by IDA. The remaining US$50 million in PCM is expected to comprise US$10 million in equity and US$40 million in debt. The study also identified the need for risk-mitigation instruments, including a potential future payment risk guarantee financed through IDA.
18. The project is aligned with the WBG Strategy on Water Security, the Water Strategy Implementation
Plan (WSIP) and the WBG Action Plan on Climate Change Adaptation and Resilience 2021–2025. The project directly supports the WSIP24 by expanding access to WASH under the “water for people” pillar of the Water
Forward Initiative. On mitigation, the project will improve energy and water efficiency through NRW reduction and operational efficiency measures. On adaptation, it will strengthen resilience by developing climate-resilient infrastructure and protecting water and sanitation assets from floods, droughts, and landslides.
19. The project is aligned with the WBG’s Gender Strategy 2024–2030.25 It will improve health and education
outcomes for women and girls by expanding household water access, reducing exposure to gender-based violence (GBV) risks, and supporting menstrual hygiene management. The project will also reduce the time and physical burden of water collection and create economic opportunities through skills development programs.
20. The project is also aligned with the WBG’s private sector development and job creation agenda. It will
provide critical WASH infrastructure for households and businesses in Kinshasa while supporting business-
enabling reforms, private sector development, and skills training. The project will create opportunities for better jobs within REGIDESO, including through utility digitalization. As a labor-intensive sector, WASH investments generate employment through construction, operations, maintenance, and supply chains, while improved services boost productivity and economic activity. The project is estimated to generate 43,118 more and better-
paid jobs (MBJ) over its lifetime, measured as project-attributable increases in labor income converted into job equivalents at baseline wages. Of these, 42,539 MBJ (99 percent) are expected from expanded water supply access and 579 MBJ from improved sanitation access.
21. The REGIDESO Center of Excellence (CoE) will establish partnerships with national academic and
vocational institutions, including the University of Kinshasa, the National Institute for Professional Education
(Institut National de Préparation Professionnelle, INPP), the National Institute for Construction and Public Works
(Institut National de Bâtiment et Travaux Publics, INBTP), (Institut de Bâtiment et Travaux Publics, IBTP) to strengthen sector skills development and ensure the sustainability of training programs beyond project closing.
The CoE will also support youth development through certification, internships, apprenticeships, and job-
readiness programs, creating a pipeline of qualified candidates for future employment within REGIDESO and the water sector.
II. PROJECT DESCRIPTION
A. Project Development Objective (PDO)
22. To increase access to climate-resilient water supply and sanitation services in Kinshasa.
PDO Level Indicators
23. Progress towards the PDO will be measured through three PDO-indicators, which also serve as Program-
level indicators (PrDO indicators) directly reporting to Corporate Results indicators.
• PDO Indicator 1: People with access to safely managed water supply services. Disaggregated by gender,
youth, (baseline: 0; target: 4.2 million) [PrDO indicator]

B. Beneficiaries
24. The project is expected to provide 4.2 million people with access to safely managed water services and
200,000 people with access to safely managed sanitation, reducing Kinshasa’s water access gap from 59 percent to 40 percent.26 Beneficiaries include: (a) residents gaining access to safely managed water services through expanded production, network extensions, and improved utility performance;27 (b) people benefiting from vocational training and job placement opportunities in water-related disciplines including employees of
REGIDESO as well as new entrants to the job market, (c) REGIDESO, through improved capacity, reduced NRW, expanded service coverage, and enhanced financial sustainability, and (d) sector institutions, including MRHE and ARPSE, through a stronger sector framework. All activities are designed to improve the resilience of communities and infrastructure to floods and droughts.
25. Given that women and girls are responsible for water collection in 72.5 percent of households,28 the
project is expected to generate significant time savings for approximately 1.6 million women and girls.29 It will also provide menstrual health and hygiene education to 9,000 girls. Students, patients and staff of 70 schools and 35 health centers in Kinshasa are expected to benefit from the installation/rehabilitation of toilet and handwashing facilities. In addition, 30,000 people, primarily internally displaced persons living in Camp Kabila, will benefit from new or rehabilitated communal WASH facilities.
C. Components
26. The project comprises three components, fully aligned with the AFE WASH MPA design and pillars. It will
establish the foundation for a phased scale-up of WASH access in Kinshasa, leveraging both private capital and development partner financing. The operation will be financed through an IDA credit of US$250 million, complemented by joint cofinancing of US$50 million from the OPEC Fund for International Development (OFID),
US$75 million from the Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa (BADEA) and US$135 million equivalent from Cassa Depositi e Prestiti (CDP) financed through the Italian Climate Fund, alongside US$15 million in counterpart financing from REGIDESO.30 In addition, the proposed hybrid PPP is expected to mobilize approximately US$50 million in private capital.

29. Component 2: Increasing Access to Climate-Resilient Water Supply and Sanitation (US$490 million total;
US$180 million IDA equivalent, US$260 million co-financing, and US$50 million in PCM) [aligned to Pillar 4 of the MPA].
• Subcomponent 2.1 Supporting Climate-Resilient Water Supply Access (US$472.7 million; US$162.7
million IDA equivalent, US$260 million co-financing, US$50 million PCM). This sub-component finances climate-resilient water supply infrastructure, including a Viability Gap Financing (VGF) grant to support a
PPP for bulk water production in Kinshasa. The investments will reduce the city’s current water production deficit by 64 percent, strengthen water security, reduce vulnerability to droughts, and enhance resilience to flooding by limiting damage to critical infrastructure and reducing contamination risks that contribute to adverse public health outcomes. It includes:
(i) Construction of a new intake on the Congo River to replace the existing flood and pollution prone intake on the N’djili River, including a transmission pipeline to the N’djili WTP;
(ii) Rehabilitation of the existing three modules of the N’djili WTP, including the construction of a meter repair and calibration workshop, to ensure resilience against flooding;
(iii) Expansion of the N’djili WTP with a fourth module of (110,000 m3/day);
(iv) Construction of a new WTP in Maluku, including intake in the Congo River and transmission pipeline, resilient to flooding
(v) Rehabilitation and expansion of distribution network infrastructure, including reservoirs and primary, secondary and tertiary networks in selected areas of Kinshasa supplied by the N’djili WTP;
(vi) Rehabilitation and expansion of distribution network infrastructure, including reservoirs and primary, secondary and tertiary networks in selected areas of Kinshasa supplied by the Ozone WTP;
(vii)Construction of new distribution network infrastructure, including reservoirs and primary, secondary and tertiary networks in a selected area of Kinshasa supplied by a future WTP in the Maluku area;
(viii) A Viability Gap Financing (VGF) grant will support the financial viability of the Lukunga bulk water
PPP. The VGF may be provided as (a) a capital subsidy to the competitively selected Special Purpose
Vehicle (SPV) responsible for the design, financing, construction, operation, and transfer of the treatment plants, and/or (b) an equity contribution by the State and/or REGIDESO in the SPV. A transaction advisor, financed under the AGREE Project, will support the Government in structuring and conducting the competitive tender process, evaluating bids, selecting the preferred bidder, and finalizing the PPP Agreement, Bulk Water Supply Agreement, and related legal, financing, guarantee, and financial arrangements required for financial close. The Project includes an indicative IDA-
financed VGF envelope of US$37 million. The final VGF requirement will be determined through competitive tendering, with the contract awarded to the compliant bidder requiring the lowest VGF subsidy while meeting the specified technical, service, and bulk water tariff requirements acceptable to REGIDESO as off-taker. IFC and MIGA are expected to provide stapled financing and guarantee terms as part of the PPP tender package.
(ix) Engineering and construction supervision services for investments under subcomponent 2.1.

• Subcomponent 2.2 – Sanitation and WASH access in institutions (US$17.3 million IDA equivalent). This
subcomponent will support implementation of the CWIS Master Plan by financing (i) the preparation of detailed technical studies for priority sanitation infrastructure, including additional wastewater and fecal sludge treatment plants to reduce GHG emissions and protect water resources; and (ii) TA, works, training, and equipment for no-regret investments, including (a) climate-resilient WASH facilities in schools and health centers, together with menstrual hygiene management activities for girls; (b)

D. Rationale for Bank Involvement and Role of Partners
31. The World Bank’s engagement is grounded in its comparative advantage in supporting complex,
infrastructure programs in FCV and low-capacity environments. The World Bank brings extensive global and regional experience in designing and implementing WASH programs, particularly in contexts that require institutional and governance reforms. DRC will benefit extensively from Phase I of the regional MPA (P506439), implemented by AUDA-NEPAD. AUDA-NEPAD will engage global and regional knowledge partners to deliver TA, analytics, and peer-to-peer exchanges through a learning agenda tailored to the DRC context. Hence, the World
Bank’s involvement is critical to assist the government with knowledge to (a) advance institutional reforms and regulatory competencies; (b) enhance utility performance through energy efficiency, digitalization, and NRW
The World Bank
Accelerating Access to Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in the Eastern and Southern Africa Region (P512763) –
Phase 4
Page 27 measures; (c) prepare the hybrid PPP; (d) achieve good international practice relating to E&S sustainability, and
(e) integrate climate adaptation and mitigation measures in infrastructure design and operations.
32. The World Bank is an active participant in the WASH sectoral coordination group, which ensures
alignment of development partner interventions with government priorities. The World Bank’s convening and technical leadership roles are instrumental in harmonizing efforts and scaling up impact in the sector. The project is designed to complement and leverage the efforts of key development partners active in DRC’s WASH sector, specifically the UNICEF, AFD, AfDB, KfW-GIZ, OFID, Italian Cooperation (CDP), and BADEA. E. Lessons Learned Reflected in the Project Design
33. The project design draws lessons from the World Bank’s global and regional WASH portfolio, the AFE
WASH Access MPA (P512763) learning agenda, and implementation experience under KIN ELENDA (P171141),
PASEA (P178389), and AGREE (P173506) in DRC. These lessons have directly informed the project’s architecture, implementation arrangements, and risk mitigation measures.
34. Key lessons reflected in the design include: (i) the need for sustained institutional support and phased
reforms to strengthen REGIDESO; (ii) the use of performance-based management and Key Performance Indicator monitoring to improve utility accountability, service quality, and financial sustainability; (iii) the importance of well-structured hybrid PPPs, combining transaction advisory support, viability gap funding, and other de-risking instruments to mobilize private capital; (iv) the adoption of digital solutions, including SCADA, Management
Information Systems, and customer engagement platforms, to improve efficiency, transparency, and NRW reduction; (v) targeted gender interventions to reduce women’s time burden, expand access to safely managed services, and promote female employment in the sector; and (vi) the integration of climate-resilient infrastructure and adaptation measures from the outset.
35. Whereas the AFE WASH MPA learning agenda has not yet started, the program has been influential in
shaping the operation through lessons learned from the already approved phases and the program priority framework. Key lessons/priorities incorporated in this project include (a) need for policy and regulatory reforms, particularly in FCV contexts, and providing institutional support to state-owned enterprises (REGIDESO); (b)
contributing to the regional benchmarking of MPA-participating countries in terms of progress on the systems change agenda; (c) documenting utility turnaround toward financial viability, including lessons on opportunities for hybrid PPP models; (d) evaluating the effectiveness of digital tools in improving NRW and overall utility performance; (e) assessing the impact of WASH interventions on girls’/women’s time burden; and (f) generating
The World Bank
Accelerating Access to Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in the Eastern and Southern Africa Region (P512763) –
Phase 4
Page 28 evidence on the cost-effectiveness and scalability of climate-resilient water infrastructure. The proposed interventions are designed not only to deliver results in DRC, but also to generate evidence on the effectiveness of the interventions at regional level. Through the MPA’s knowledge, evaluation, and learning platform, project results will contribute to regional benchmarking and systems-change assessments, and the lessons generated in
DRC will inform future MPA phases and similar operations across Africa.
III. PROJECT IMPLEMENTATION
A. Institutional and Implementation Arrangements
36. A Project Steering Committee (PSC) that includes the key ministries and agencies involved in the Project
will be set up to provide strategic guidance during project implementation. The PSC will guide project implementation, approve annual work plans and budgets, and facilitate coordination among the ministries and institutions involved in the Project. The PSC will be chaired by the Ministry of Water Resources and Electricity
(MRHE), represented by the Secretary General of MRHE. The Ministry of the Environment, Sustainable
Development and New Climate Economy (MEDDNEC) will serve as vice-chair of this committee, represented by the Secretary General of the MEDDNEC. Its membership will include representatives of the Presidency, the Prime
Minister’s Office, the Ministries of Finance (Cellule de Suivi des Projets et Programmes, CSPP), Planning, Portfolio
(Comité de Pilotage de la Réforme des Entreprises du Portefeuille de l'Etat, COPIREP), Health, Education, Urbanism and Housing, Land Affairs, the Governorate of the Ville-Province de Kinshasa (VPK), REGIDESO, ARSPE, and the
CEP-O Coordinator. CEP-O will serve as the secretariat of the PSC.
37. CEP-O, hosted within the MRHE, will serve as the Project Implementation Unit (PIU) responsible for
implementation of all Project activities. CEP-O will be responsible for project management, procurement, technical quality control, contract management, implementation oversight, financial management, E&S risk management, monitoring and evaluation, reporting, coordination, and liaison with the PSC. CEP-O will prepare and consolidate project work plans and budgets, oversee implementation across all components, manage project funds, and ensure compliance with World Bank requirements. CEP-O is already staffed with the specialists required for project implementation.
38. For the water supply component, CEP-O’s technical staff will be complemented by a team of technical
experts from REGIDESO’s Projects and Works Directorate, comprising REGIDESO staff and additional specialists
(consultants). The team will provide technical support to CEP-O in the preparation and review of technical specifications, engineering studies, bidding documents, cost estimates, technical designs, participation in evaluation committees, and implementation monitoring, with the objective of strengthening technical quality and project management capacity. CEP-O will remain solely responsible for project implementation as mentioned above. A collaboration agreement between CEP-O and REGIDESO will clearly define the scope of collaboration, including the roles and responsibilities of each party, as well as the specific expertise, TA, and support to be provided by the technical experts.
39. For the hybrid PPP, the SPV will be responsible for financing, design, construction, commissioning,
operation, and maintenance of the bulk water production facilities. A concession agreement (or similar PPP contract), a bulk water supply agreement, and any other agreements required for the financing, implementation, operation, maintenance, and support of the facilities will be entered into among REGIDESO, the selected private partner (through the SPV), and other relevant government entities, as applicable. Collectively, these agreements and instruments will constitute the PPP Transaction Documents. CEP-O will lead the competitive procurement of the private partner in accordance with World Bank procurement requirements and will provide overall oversight, coordination, and consolidated reporting through financial close and throughout project implementation. The
SPV will enter into a Subsidiary Agreement with the Government and a Project Agreement with IDA, setting out
The World Bank
Accelerating Access to Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in the Eastern and Southern Africa Region (P512763) –
Phase 4
Page 29 the terms of the VGF support and ensuring compliance with the applicable World Bank Environmental and Social
Standards.
40. For sanitation-related activities, CEP-O will likewise retain full responsibility for project implementation
and will coordinate technical inputs from the relevant national and provincial entities. The VPK, through the
CDUK and other specialized provincial services (RASKIN, REGEDEK, BSPE, and FONAK), will provide technical support to CEP-O during project preparation and implementation. This support may include assistance with technical specifications, participation in evaluation committees, technical review of designs, monitoring of sanitation investments, incorporation of urban resilience considerations, and engagement with local stakeholders and provincial authorities. A dedicated Sanitation expert will be recruited and seconded to CDUK to facilitate coordination and technical support. The DAS of the MEDDNEC will provide policy oversight to ensure that the national standards are respected. CEP-O will coordinate these inputs as part of its overall responsibility for project implementation and reporting.
41. Specialized technical entities will support implementation in their respective areas of mandate. UC-PPP
and ARSPE will support PPP-related activities, including reviewing relevant procurement and consultation documents, participation in evaluation processes, and monitoring of PPP contractual arrangements. COPIREP will support activities related to the continued reform and transformation of REGIDESO. The entities responsible for health facilities, schools, roads, urban planning, and land administration, will contribute to technical review, permitting, land allocation, monitoring, and supervision within their respective mandates. The detailed roles, responsibilities, membership of the PSC, and coordination arrangements will be further specified in the Project
Implementation Manual (PIM).
42. To ensure coordination with Phase I of the AFE WASH Access MPA, a representative of MRHE has been
assigned to the Regional Project Advisory Committee to ensure that MPA activities are well scoped and add value to the project.
B. Results Monitoring, Evaluation, and Verification Arrangements
43. CEP-O will be responsible for overall M&E of the project. A dedicated M&E specialist will lead data
collection, consolidation, analysis, and reporting against the Results Framework, providing regular updates on progress toward outcomes. CEP-O will coordinate with REGIDESO, CDUK, and the specialized entities to ensure timely and accurate reporting. Component 3 will finance M&E capacity building and baseline and end-point surveys. CEP-O will establish and manage the M&E system, including: (a) collection and reporting of results data, disaggregated by gender and age; (b) beneficiary surveys and technical audits to validate service delivery outcomes, including impacts on women’s and girls’ time burden and perception surveys to track the impact of improved water and sanitation services on community trust in the state as a service provider; (c) midterm and completion evaluations to assess results, sustainability, and lessons learned. CEP-O will submit semi-annual progress reports, as well as midterm and completion reports, to the World Bank. M&E findings will be used throughout implementation to monitor progress, address emerging challenges, and inform future operations.
C. Sustainability
44. Institutional and Financial Sustainability. The project strengthens governance, institutional capacity, and
utility performance to enhance sector sustainability. Implementation of REGIDESO’s PIP, digitalization, and accountability measures will improve operational efficiency, revenue collection, and reduce NRW. Tariff and financing studies will guide future reforms, while co-financing and hybrid PPPs will help mobilize private capital.
45. Technical Sustainability and Climate Resilience. Sustainability is supported through climate-resilient
investments in water production and distribution infrastructure, designed to withstand flood and drought risks.
Digital tools, including SCADA systems, will improve efficiency and service reliability. Capacity building,
The World Bank
Accelerating Access to Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in the Eastern and Southern Africa Region (P512763) –
Phase 4
Page 30 knowledge transfer under works and PPP contracts, and investments based on master plans, feasibility studies, and detailed designs will strengthen long-term operation and maintenance.
46. Environmental and Social Sustainability. Environmental and social considerations are integrated into
project design through application of the WBG Environmental and Social Framework (ESF). The project will screen all subproject activities for E&S risks and impacts, and prepare Environmental and Social Impact Assessments
(ESIA), Environmental and Social Management Plans (ESMP) and Resettlement Action Plans (RAP), a Stakeholder
Engagement Plan (SEP), Labor Management and Operational Health and Safety Procedures, and other instruments as needed to ensure an effective and inclusive implementation and management of E&S risks and impacts, including Sexual Exploitation and Abuse/Sexual Harassment (SEA/SH) risks. Citizen engagement and communication activities will support service expansion, promote responsible water use, and reduce vandalism.
IV. PROJECT APPRAISAL SUMMARY
A. Technical, Economic and Financial Analysis
47. The project design incorporates a phased, climate-resilient and inclusive approach to address critical gaps
in WSS infrastructure and service delivery in Kinshasa. The project is structured around three components that collectively aim to strengthen institutional frameworks, improve service provider performance, expand access, and ensure effective project coordination and management. The technical design prioritizes investments to urgently increase production capacity, through new climate-proof water intakes for water treatment plants on the Congo River, as well as transmission lines, reservoirs, and rehabilitation and expansion of the distribution network. The project, through TA, also reinforces the roles of key institutions such as REGIDESO and the sanitation institutions in the city.
48. The technical design is underpinned by feasibility studies, assessments, and climate risk screening. Key
technical features include the following:
(a) Climate-resilient infrastructure. Water supply investments are designed to withstand floods, droughts, and landslides. Replacing the N’djili tributary intake with a Congo River intake for the N’djili and Lukunga WTPs will improve resilience by reducing exposure to highly polluted and sediment-laden water during flood events.
(b) Digitalization and operational efficiency. Investments include SCADA, digital customer tools, and energy-efficient upgrades to reduce NRW and improve service quality, as prioritized in REGIDESO’s PIP.
(c) Inclusive sanitation follows the CWIS approach, integrating household demand creation with support to professionalize local FSM operators. Investments include a fecal sludge treatment plant, behavior change interventions, and durable sanitation facilities in military camps, schools, and health centers, complemented by menstrual hygiene education to support girls’ empowerment and school attendance.
49. Preparation activities financed under KIN ELENDA (P171141) and AGREE (P173506) have substantially
advanced project readiness. Detailed designs for the water supply investments are complete or well advanced, and procurement is underway for the N’djili works package (approximately US$200 million), with contract award expected before project effectiveness. For the Lukunga hybrid PPP (approximately US$88 million), the transaction advisor is being recruited under AGREE, while reference designs and bidding documents are expected to be finalized by June 2027. For sanitation, detailed designs and bidding documents for the fecal sludge treatment plant have been completed and procurement is underway. The ESIA and RAP for the N’djili works are expected to be completed by May 2027. An implementation plan has been prepared, with about 40 percent of civil works expected to commence within the first year of implementation. CEP-O has demonstrated implementation
The World Bank
Accelerating Access to Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in the Eastern and Southern Africa Region (P512763) –
Phase 4
Page 31 capacity through the ongoing projects and will be further reinforced by REGIDESO technical experts and a dedicated CDUK sanitation specialist, expected to be in place by credit effectiveness.
Economic Assessment
50. Economic analysis. An economic analysis was carried out to assess the economic viability of the project,
and the results confirm the strong justification for the proposed investments. The cost-benefit analysis (CBA)
evaluates the economic costs and benefits of water supply and sanitation investments under a 30-year time horizon using a 6 percent discount rate. The analysis includes (a) total project costs, comprising capital investments, operation and maintenance (O&M), and replacement costs, as well as TA and project management expenditures, and (b) all quantifiable benefits, including reduced incidence of waterborne diseases, healthcare cost savings, and significant time savings for households and caregivers.
51. The project is expected to deliver substantial economic and social benefits by expanding access to climate-
resilient water supply services to approximately 4.2 million people and sanitation services to about 200,000 people in Kinshasa. In addition to quantified benefits, the project generates important non-monetized benefits, including an improved social contract between the state and citizens as service provider, improved environmental quality, protection of water resources, enhanced climate resilience, reduced pollution from untreated fecal sludge, strengthened institutional capacity, improved educational outcomes through better
WASH facilities in schools, and positive gender impacts, particularly for women and girls.
52. Economic efficiency and climate co-benefits. The efficiency analysis yields strong results, confirming the
project’s economic viability. The aggregated economic analysis estimates an Economic Net Present Value (ENPV)
of approximately US$1.48 billion and an Economic Internal Rate of Return (EIRR) of 33.2 percent, and a benefit-
cost ratio exceeding 3.09, indicating that the economic benefits significantly outweigh the costs. The water supply component generates most of the benefits, reflecting large gains from improved service reliability and reduced time spent collecting water, while the sanitation component also contributes positively through health improvements and environmental benefits.
53. The economic analysis incorporates greenhouse gas (GHG) accounting using both high and low Shadow
Price of Carbon scenarios. Results show that the project will lead to a net reduction in emissions of approximately
-715,400 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent over its lifetime (about –23,850 tonnes annually), driven mainly by reduced
reliance on boiling water and improved wastewater management. The inclusion of climate externalities does not materially alter the economic results, as the magnitude of emission reductions, while positive, remains modest relative to the overall economic benefits.
54. The sensitivity analysis confirms the robustness of the project’s economic viability under a range of
adverse scenarios. The analysis was conducted to test the robustness of the CBA results under changes in key parameters, including investment cost overruns, O&M costs, individual benefit categories (time savings and health benefits), the Shadow Price of Carbon (SPC), and the discount rate. The results demonstrate that the project's economic viability is not highly sensitive to variations in any of these parameters. Switching value analysis shows that investment costs would need to increase by more than 350 percent, O&M costs by more than
645 percent, or the discount rate by more than 500 percent before the project would cease to generate a positive net present value. The project's economic returns are thus robust across a wide range of adverse scenarios.
55. Financial analysis. The financial and economic analysis assessed the feasibility of mobilizing private capital
for bulk water production through a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) for the proposed Lukunga (100,000 m³/day)
and Maluku (110,000 m³/day) water treatment plants, with a combined capacity of approximately 210,000 m³/day and annual production of about 69 million m³. The analysis was based on a medium-growth scenario reflecting realistic improvements in service coverage, operational performance, and customer growth. Under this scenario, water service coverage in Kinshasa is projected to increase from about 50 percent today to 61 percent
